title: The Strait of Hormuz: A Water Highway That's Causing Big Trouble
summary:
Imagine a water highway so important that one-fifth of the world's oil travels through it every day. That's the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea passage between Iran and other countries. In February, the U.S. and Israel started a war with Iran. Iran fought back by closing the strait, which made oil prices jump around the world.

Now, the U.S. says it has made progress. It has stopped Iran from selling its own oil and helped other countries in the Gulf send more oil through the strait. Iran's oil exports dropped from 1.85 million barrels a day to just 255,000 in August. Non-Iranian oil exports rose from 300,000 barrels a day to 10.8 million in September.

But the war is not over. It has cost the U.S. more than $37.5 billion and 18 American service members have died. Iran is still attacking ships. Its allies, the Houthis in Yemen, are attacking Saudi Arabia's oil facilities. This has pushed oil prices above $100 a barrel, and diesel hit a record high. That means higher prices for gas, food, and many things people buy.

Experts say neither side is winning. "The war is likely to be protracted with no clear victor," said Mona Yacoubian, a Middle East expert. President Trump said gas prices will likely stay high through the November elections. The big question: how does this end?
why_it_matters: When oil becomes more expensive, the price of gas, food, and other things your family buys usually goes up too.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz (a narrow waterway between the Persian Gulf and the open ocean) is one of the most important oil routes on Earth — about one-fifth of the world's oil is shipped through it.
Iran (a large country in the Middle East) and the United States have been enemies for many years, and their ships have clashed in the Gulf before, back in the 1980s.
The Houthis (a fighting group in Yemen, a country at the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula) have been attacking ships and oil sites in the region for years.
Article_Structure: WHO: The United States, Israel, and Iran, plus Iran's allies the Houthis in Yemen, who attack Saudi Arabia's oil facilities.
WHAT: Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz and oil prices jumped; the U.S. says it stopped Iran from selling its own oil and helped other Gulf countries send more oil through the strait.
WHERE: The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea passage between Iran and other countries, and Saudi Arabia's oil facilities.
WHY: The fighting is pushing up the price of oil, gas, and food, and experts say neither side is winning.

perspectives.perspective: The U.S. and its Gulf partners
perspectives.description: They say Iran closing the water highway hurt the whole world, so blocking Iran's oil sales and keeping other countries' oil flowing helps keep prices from getting even worse.
They see the strait and the attacks as a way to strike back at the U.S. and Israel and to show they cannot be ignored.
Mona Yacoubian and others say the war is likely to be protracted with no clear victor, so the fighting could drag on with no easy ending.
